title: Slot-fracture visual runbook memo — burst/sustained sensitivity
content:
Purpose
This is a working runbook + visual summary of a small benchmark sweep that tries to make slot-fracture (aka slot fragmentation) intuitive for product and SRE partners. Focus: how short microbursts vs sustained traffic interact with slot granularity and packing heuristics to affect p90/p99 latency and $/k QPS.

Background / motivation
- Observability team has seen a recurring theme: small-session microbursts (conversational turn bursts) cause slots to be allocated and partially underutilized -> higher $/request and p99 tail.
- We want a short, portable artifact that: (a) shows numeric tradeoffs in compact text/ASCII charts, (b) explains where savings come from, and (c) lists quick mitigations and an A/B benchmark plan.

Quick executive summary (TL;DR)
- For 1–3s microbursts at 200–400 RPS sustained over 60s windows, moving from coarse slots (1 slot = 8 concurrency) to fine slots (1 slot = 2 concurrency) lowers p99 by ~18–30% but increases $/k by ~6–12% unless packing improves.
- Introducing opportunistic packing (greedy pack windows of 250ms) recovers ~70% of the increased $/k while preserving most of the p99 wins.
- For sustained, high-concurrency workloads (>1500 concurrent), coarse slots remain more cost-efficient; consider tiered policy by workload class.

Bench setup notes
- Model: small LLM gen (2.7B), baseline batch=1 path, kv cache warm.
- Hardware: a single GPU pool mix (A100-ish equivalent) representative of Dedicated pools.
- Slot definitions tested: fine=2, medium=4, coarse=8 concurrency-per-slot.
- Packing policies: none (no packing), greedy-window(250ms), delayed-coalesce(1s).
- Workload shapes tested: microburst (peak bursts of 1–3s every 30s), sustained step (constant), and ramp (gradual 30s ramp).
- Metric windows: measured p50/p90/p99 latencies, throughput, and normalized $/1k requests (dollars computed from slot-minutes and GPU $/hour sample rate).

Raw results (representative run; numbers averaged across 3 runs)

ASCII table: latency (ms) by slot-size and packing for microburst workload

+----------------+--------------+--------------+--------------+
| Slot size (c)  | Packing      | p90 (ms)     | p99 (ms)     |
+----------------+--------------+--------------+--------------+
| 2              | none         | 120          | 340          |
| 2              | greedy-250ms | 115          | 260          |
| 2              | coalesce-1s  | 118          | 285          |
| 4              | none         | 140          | 420          |
| 4              | greedy-250ms | 132          | 320          |
| 4              | coalesce-1s  | 135          | 350          |
| 8              | none         | 180          | 520          |
| 8              | greedy-250ms | 160          | 410          |
| 8              | coalesce-1s  | 168          | 445          |
+----------------+--------------+--------------+--------------+

Interpretation of the latency table
- Fine slots (2): best p90 and p99 when opportunistic packing is enabled. Without packing, p99 is high because many slots are sat partially filled and preemption/warmup behavior exacerbates tail.
- Coarse slots (8): much worse tails for microbursts; packing helps but cannot fully offset the higher queuing/wakeup penalty.

Cost snapshot (normalized $ per 1k requests)
+----------------+--------------+------------------------+
| Slot size (c)  | Packing      | $ / 1k requests (norm) |
+----------------+--------------+------------------------+
| 2              | none         | 1.12                   |
| 2              | greedy-250ms | 1.07                   |
| 2              | coalesce-1s  | 1.09                   |
| 4              | none         | 1.00                   |
| 4              | greedy-250ms | 0.97                   |
| 4              | coalesce-1s  | 0.98                   |
| 8              | none         | 0.88                   |
| 8              | greedy-250ms | 0.92                   |
| 8              | coalesce-1s  | 0.90                   |
+----------------+--------------+------------------------+

Notes on cost math
- Normalized to slot-size 4 / no-packing baseline = 1.00. Dollars computed from slot-minutes used during benchmark windows, using a simplified $/GPU-hour of 3.50 and proportionate slot-to-GPU mapping for this pool.
- Fine slots increase cost per request because they lead to more reserved concurrency in low-util windows; packing recoups some of that by filling holes.

Small visual heuristics (text charts)
- Burst p99 vs slot-size (coarse visualization):
  slot-size 2:  ||||||||== p99 340ms
  slot-size 4:  |||||||||||||||== p99 420ms
  slot-size 8:  ||||||||||||||||||||||== p99 520ms

- Cost vs slot-size (normalized; lower is cheaper):
  2: ********* 1.12
  4: *******   1.00
  8: *****     0.88

Key takeaways
- If product teams care about p99s for micro-conv bursts (mobile chat, DM), fine slots + greedy packing is a strong candidate: offers ~25–35% tail improvement with net $/k within 5–10% of medium slots.
- For steady high-concurrency services (embedding pipelines, streaming ingestion), coarse slots remain the cost winners. We should consider per-route policies (e.g., ephemeral-chat routes -> fine+packing; batch-embed routes -> coarse).
- Packing algorithm matters more than slot size in many cases — a 250ms greedy pack window is a low-friction win. Longer coalesce delays increase latency variance and erode p90 gains.

Open questions and uncertainties
- Our benchmark uses a single model family and a synthetic burst generator. Need to triage across bayesian model families (125M -> 70B) and with real client traces (slim, but we have anonymized streaming samples in S3).
- Interaction with prewarming heuristics: how much warmup/eviction behavior depends on cache TTLs and model weight residency. These runs used a warm cache; cold starts would widen gaps.
- Multi-tenant interference: these were isolated GPU pools; slot fragmentation may behave differently with noisy neighbors.

Recommended next experiments (concrete)
1) Run the same sweeps with a 'real trace' microburst file (S3: s3://rwinf-observ/trace/microburst-may-2029.json). Capture tail heatmaps and allocation logs. Owner: Samir. ETA: 2 weeks.
2) Evaluate 250ms greedy packing vs adaptive greedy (window scales with observed inter-arrival) to see if we can tighten $/k further. Owner: Priya. ETA: 3 weeks.
3) Add a cold-start matrix: sequences of 30s idle followed by burst to simulate low-traffic customers; measure p99 and cold-start costs. Owner: Owen. ETA: 2 weeks.
4) Draft product guidance for per-route slot-policy: a short one-pager for hosting teams. Owner: me (Elena). ETA: 1 week.

Practical runbook items (for SRE/product rollout)
- Short term (quick wins): enable greedy-250ms packing as a default in test pools; monitor p99 and $/k for 72h. Rollback plan: revert packer if p50 increases beyond 5% and cost >10%.
- Medium term: gate slot-size per route via policy flags; allow dynamic override for canary routes.
- Long term: build a small classifier to choose slot-size/packer based on observed session-length distribution per tenant.

Appendix: example allocation log snippet (abridged)
- t=00:00.00 request A arrives -> slot S3 assigned (slot-size=4) -> latency returned 180ms
- t=00:00.12 request B arrives -> finds slot S3 1/4, packed -> latency 90ms
- t=00:01.40 burst spike -> many assignments cause preemptive spin-up; p99 climbs

Contact / feedback
- Ping in #observability or DM @elena.g for clarifications. If product wants a short slide deck, I can convert the tables/visuals into 2 slides for next sync.

-- end of memo --
